segments.narration: For three days in 1883, the sun burned blue. Astronomers panicked, and citizens across the globe looked up in terror.
In August 1883, the Indonesian volcanic island of Krakatoa completely blew apart. But the real shockwave wasn't local—it went global.
The eruption's energy yield was four times greater than the largest thermonuclear bomb ever detonated. How did sound waves circle the Earth more than three times?
Trillions of microscopic ash particles shot miles high into the stratosphere, forming a permanent global haze that choked out normal daylight.
Those exact ash particles acted as a giant optical filter. They scattered red and yellow light away, leaving only blue wavelengths to pierce the sky.
